question: What are the ways to perform optomechincal cooling

ingredients.name: answer_critical_0
ingredients.criterion: The answer must state that quantum control of a mechanical oscillator requires it to be in or near its quantum ground state (low thermal phonon occupation), and that dilution refrigerator temperatures (~20 mK) are insufficient unless the mechanical frequency is in the GHz range, motivating additional cooling schemes.
examples: Optomechanical quantum control requires the oscillator in or near its ground state
At 20 mK, only GHz-frequency nanomechanical modes satisfy kBT << hbar*Omega_m
Additional cooling of the selected mechanical mode is needed

ingredients.name: answer_critical_1
ingredients.criterion: The answer must define optomechanical cooling as exploiting the coupling between light confined in an optical cavity/resonator and mechanical motion, with radiation pressure providing the physical mechanism for removing energy from the mechanical mode.
examples: Radiation pressure of light confined in a resonator exerts forces on a moving mirror
An optical field couples to mechanical motion, reducing its effective temperature

ingredients.name: answer_critical_2
ingredients.criterion: The answer must distinguish two main types of optomechanical cooling: feedback cooling and intrinsic cavity (radiation-pressure) cooling.
examples: There exist two main types: feedback cooling and intrinsic cavity cooling
Optomechanical cooling can be classified into feedback-based and back-action-based schemes

ingredients.name: answer_critical_3
ingredients.criterion: The answer must describe feedback cooling as using optical read-out of mechanical motion and a feedback loop that applies a radiation-pressure damping force (cold damping) to the oscillator.
examples: A feedback loop between mechanical motion and radiation-pressure force provides damping
Cold damping based on real-time measurement of displacement

ingredients.name: answer_critical_4
ingredients.criterion: The answer must describe intrinsic cavity cooling via dynamic back-action arising from the finite cavity decay time, in which a red-detuned laser field's radiation pressure absorbs thermal phonons and damps the mechanical vibration.
examples: A red-detuned laser absorbs thermal phonons and suppresses vibration
Back-action cooling arises from dynamic back-action due to finite cavity decay time

ingredients.name: valuable_0
ingredients.criterion: The answer should cite quantitative demonstrations, e.g., feedback cooling from room temperature to 1.2 mK (~27 phonons) in an integrated optomechanical structure, and GHz-frequency devices reaching the quantum regime by cryogenics alone.
examples: Cooling from room temperature to 1.2 mK, fewer than 27 phonons (fm*Qm ~ 2.6e13)
GHz nanomechanical setups (Chan et al. 2011; Eichenfield et al. 2009)

ingredients.name: valuable_1
ingredients.criterion: The answer should note that back-action cooling and parametric instability are two sides of the same dynamic back-action mechanism, and that the mechanism is general to any mechanical oscillator parametrically coupled to an electromagnetic resonator.
examples: Parametric instability and back-action cooling are two sides of dynamic back-action
The same phenomena occur for oscillators parametrically coupled to electromagnetic resonators

ingredients.name: valuable_2
ingredients.criterion: The answer may mention device-level enablers (high mechanical quality factor, large optomechanical coupling, suppression of bending losses) and that radiation-pressure coupling first arose in gravitational-wave interferometry with Braginsky predicting dynamic back-action.
examples: Fishbone-like photonic/phononic structure with Gom/2pi ~ 21.6 GHz/nm and fm*Qm ~ 2.6e13
Braginsky's pioneering work predicted dynamic back-action effects in interferometric gravitational-wave experiments

ingredients.name: valuable_3
ingredients.criterion: The answer may note that recent nanomechanical setups use GHz-range mechanical frequencies, for which cryogenic cooling alone can approach the ground state.
examples: GHz-frequency nanomechanical setups reduce initial thermal occupation at 20 mK
Cryogenic ground-state cooling of GHz mechanical modes

ingredients.name: valuable_4
ingredients.criterion: The answer may discuss the practical limits of each approach, e.g., measurement imprecision and feedback bandwidth limits in cold damping, and the quantum back-action / resolved-sideband limit in cavity cooling.
examples: Cavity cooling is limited by quantum back-action and requires resolved-sideband operation
Feedback cooling performance is limited by measurement imprecision and delay
